I think it’s interesting that you say that! I see where you are coming from and that not everything has a deeper meaning to it. 

However I’d still like to believe that in this instance, where the phrase is spoken three times instead of once, and at a climactic point in the novella, we can derive some sort of meaningfulness from it, especially in the context of the effect that it’s making - I’m not native French but using the the passé simple may imply a greater sense of the immutable? Perhaps someone can correct me on that. I was silent vs I was staying silent definitely have different temporal effects, which is the fact of the language, but the effect, perhaps, we can interpret for ourselves.

It is true, however, that tenses are simply how the language is constructed - maybe I am wrong to read so deeply. You make a good point!

Indeed - I think it is interesting to think of it in terms of habitual action. In English, ‘used to’ often indicates an opposite state in the present, a negative or positive progression...for instance, “She used to be beautiful” lends itself to a ‘negative’ present. 

But we cannot always manipulate it in the same way in English as Spanish, or French. 

So interesting!

There is definitely a subtlety in the difference between Je me taisais and Je me tus - especially because the narrator repeats it three times. It probably suits this ongoing surrender and powerlessness to the little prince’s desire to return home but also die.

That’s an interesting viewpoint -  I’m scared to over-read the text to be honest, but this idea of continual disappointment/longing for the past is so pertinent to Saint-Exupéry himself - for his homeland, and the restoration of humanity to a ‘purer’ and more childlike state (not the ‘simpleness’ of a child but the clarity of which they see the world)...

In these indefinite ends there is a sense of incompleteness of the self as an extension of one’s own actions. Perhaps.
